leads.headline: The Long Beach Company Was Probably McDonnell Douglas
leads.claim: In his FASTWALKERS video Gerb takes the source Ross Coulthart quotes in In Plain Sight, who described 'an aerospace company in Long Beach California' with sprawling gardens and access to crash wreckage, and matches it to the Aerospace Corporation, calling it 'the only major Aerospace company in Long Beach California that has this type of Campus'. The vault's own Aerospace Corporation page says that company is headquartered in El Segundo and finds no Long Beach campus for it. The major aerospace company in Long Beach was Douglas Aircraft, whose Long Beach plant became McDonnell Douglas's main airliner and transport works from 1967 and Boeing's after 1997. Two other videos point the same way without ever mentioning Long Beach. In UFOs in the Private Sector - Lockheed Martin, Gerb plays Gary Nolan saying well-informed people told him crash materials sit with contractors, naming 'McDonald Douglas' first. In the Majestic-12 video, Ryan Wood says his father Robert Wood got Douglas Aircraft management to spend internal R&D money on UFO propulsion around 1967, carried through the McDonnell Douglas merger. Inference: Coulthart's Long Beach company fits McDonnell Douglas (or its successor at the site, Boeing) better than the Aerospace Corporation, and that would tie Coulthart's source, Nolan's remark and the Woods' story to the same firm.

leads.claim: Witness Ed (11063) spent 2010 to 2015 at the Pentagon. In The Hidden Wing Gerb places him in Air Force acquisition (SAF/AQ), where Ed says 30 to 40 percent of Air Force total obligation authority was moved into the black budget before financial management could review it, and Greer's notes give the sums as $34 billion and then $40 billion, which Gerb dates to fiscal years 2013 and 2014. In his separate MITRE video Gerb profiles William LaPlante, who left MITRE in 2013 to run that same office as Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Acquisition and then went back to MITRE to run its National Security Engineering Center. So the head of SAF/AQ during Ed's last Pentagon years, and during the fiscal years of the transfers Ed describes, was a MITRE executive who left MITRE for the post and returned to it afterwards. Gerb never puts Ed and LaPlante in the same passage; the only Ed-MITRE tie he draws is Ed's earlier posting to Hanscom.

Put together: Cardillo was the first holder of that same DDNI/II post (2010-2014), so he served directly under DNI Clapper beside O'Sullivan, and Dempsey was his successor. Before that, Cardillo was DIA deputy director (2006-2010), which covers the September 2008 award of AAWSAP, the DIA program meant to receive the material, and the 2008-09 attempt, when Clapper was Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence over the DIA. The two blocked transfers that Gerb treats as separate events both ran through one Clapper-Cardillo chain of command, and the post Gerb counts among Clapper's 'goons' was Cardillo's before it was Dempsey's.

In UAP Reverse Engineering at Edwards Air Force Base it is 'the alleged 1957 Hollman Air Force Base Landing', mentioned in the same stretch of the video as Gordon Cooper's 1957 Edwards lakebed landing, which may be where the year came from. The 1957 date also lines up with Corso's own claimed alien encounter at Red Canyon on the White Sands range next to Holloman, which Gerb dates to 1957-58 in the Corso video without connecting the two. leads.headline: Grusch's Clapper timeline starts in 1991, not 2009
leads.claim: Gerb consistently casts James Clapper as the man who 'picked up the pieces' of the legacy programs after Dick Cheney left office in January 2009. But in the Megyn Kelly clip Gerb plays in at least three videos, Grusch says Clapper managed the crash retrieval issue 'when he was the DNI, USDI and DIA director'. Clapper ran the DIA from November 1991 to August 1995 (vault Clapper page) and was USD(I) from 2007 to 2010, so by Grusch's own words Clapper's role began during Cheney's tenure as Secretary of Defense and ran through the 1994 restructuring that Gerb dates to the Clinton years. Two years after Clapper left DIA, the Wilson-Davis notes have Vice Admiral Thomas Wilson, then deputy DIA director/J2, refused access in 1997 by a gatekeeping structure that Gerb says was put in place in 1994. Commander Will Miller adds in 2000 that DIA directors are kept away from UAP knowledge. Put together: either Clapper's access went with him personally and not with the DIA directorship, or the 1994 reorganization is what shut DIA leadership out after Clapper left. Either way, Gerb's Cheney-then-Clapper sequence leaves out the decade Grusch himself points to.

leads.headline: Gerb's 1954 'Ka' crash puts a second saucer and bodies 25 to 30 miles from Roswell
leads.claim: In the Special Forces Confession video Gerb cites Stringfield's witness 'Ka', who on 12 April 1954 went out with a USAF crash-rescue crew from the Roswell base to a saucer crashed edgewise in sand 25 to 30 miles northwest of Roswell, found a ground crew in fatigues already tagging debris and scattered bodies, and was then debriefed for three days under threat of prison and discharge. Gerb uses Ka only as a parallel for forced secrecy and never sets the account beside Roswell itself. Lined up with the Aztec video, where the airman 'George' says the 1948 Aztec recovery was run out of Walker AFB (the renamed Roswell Army Air Field) with new people and procedures after 1947 ('no more screw-ups'), and with Haut's 2002 affidavit putting the 1947 primary site about 40 miles north of town, Ka's account means one of two things, and both matter: either the Roswell base stayed a crash-recovery launch point for years after 1947 (1947 Roswell, 1948 Aztec, 1954 Ka), with an outside team on scene before the base crew, which is the doctrine George describes; or Ka's story is a misdated 1947 impact-site account (saucer with dome, bodies, northwest of Roswell, three-day threats). The narrow, testable claim is that the videos hold a second bodies-recovered crash in the Roswell area that Gerb never connects to the 1947 case.

leads.headline: Corso's convoy came from Fort Bliss, not to it
leads.claim: In the Coyame video Gerb says that according to Corso's The Day After Roswell the Roswell debris and bodies were 'shipped to Fort Bliss Texas'. The book's account, as published reviews summarise it, has the crates arriving at Fort Riley from Fort Bliss and bound for Wright Field. Corso's own interview, played in the Corso video, says the five trucks came 'from an Airfield in in New Mexico' and were 'heading for right pison'. Fort Bliss was the convoy's origin in the book, not its destination: probably a slip of the preposition. The vault's Fort Bliss page repeats it. This matters for the published Fort Riley post too: the book routes the 6 July convoy through El Paso, a longer road trip than the straight Roswell to Fort Riley line that post measures, and the book and the interview give different origins.
